newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hillary Clinton says S.Africans inspirational.
newsitem.headline: Hillary Clinton says S.Africans inspirational.

text.p: U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Thursday praised South Africa's spirit of reconciliation in the post-apartheid period, saying the country is "too busy to hate".
President Bill Clinton's wife, in an appearance at the University of Cape Town, also predicted that the United States would elect a woman president within the next 20 years.

Speaking 31 years after U.S. Senator Robert Kennedy delivered a landmark address in South Africa on racial inequality, Mrs Clinton said Americans found inspiration in the work going on in South Africa to put the past behind it.

"We have an old saying in America that idle hands are the devil's work. From what I have seen in just a few short days, the devil will have no help here. South Africa is a country that is too busy to hate," she said.
She joined President Nelson Mandela for discussions on Thursday afternoon before a scheduled tour of Robben Island where he spent 18 of his 27 years as a political prisoner.

"I'm delighted to be here to see President Mandela again," Mrs. Clinton told reporters outside his Genadendal residence, adding that she had met Mandela in 1992 in New York before he was president and before her husband became president.
Mandela said he had thanked Mrs. Clinton for the assistance given to South Africa by the United States.
"I was very happy to meet her, Hillary, because the United States, as most of you know, has been very generous in supporting us in the apartheid struggle," he told reporters.
Mandela said the United States had also been helpful in the post-apartheid period, adding: "Our meeting has given me the opportunity to thank her."
In a question-and-answer session at the university campus earlier on Thursday, Mrs Clinton was asked whether she believed the United States would soon elect a woman as president.
She produced chuckles among the audience of students and representatives of women's groups when she replied: "I have thought a lot about this."
She said it was difficult in the United States to overcome preconceived notions and stereotypes about political leaders, and this made it hard for a woman to rise to the highest level of government.
"Having said that, I do hope and believe that sometime within the next 20 years we will have a woman president," Mrs. Clinton said.
Saying it was possible some women might run in presidential elections in the year 2000, she added there were many well-qualified women who could undertake such a campaign.

Aides to the first lady told reporters, meanwhile, that a bus meant to transport journalists accompanying Mrs. Clinton and later to be used for dignatories attending a benefit with U.S. comedian Bill Cosby on Robben Island -- had sank off Cape Town.

The 25-passenger luxury bus was being ferried from Cape Town to Robben Island by helicopter, when the holding straps broke -- plunging the bus into Table Bay where it now sits at the bottom of the sea.
